extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; creative writers studying archetypal/comic and romantic structures
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Frye's archetypal criteria for comic and romantic genres: character-types, dramatic functions, structural phases of comedy, and the formal elements of romance (quest stages, hero/antagonist polarity). Useful for literary analysis or informing creative-writing structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contest of eiron and alazon
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest of eiron and alazon forms the basis of the comic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic plots center on the conflict between the self-effacing eiron (ironic figure) and the complacent or pretentious alazon (impostor); audience sympathy typically aligns with the eiron side. Many comic scenes manifest as one character soliloquizing while another makes sarcastic asides, dramatizing this contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffoon and churl polarize comic mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Buffoon and churl (agroikos) function as polarizing mood-types in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The buffoon increases festivity and laughter, while the churl or rustic may refuse festivity and act as a killjoy; together they map the comic tone across plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senex iratus (heavy father) as alazon center
rubrics_metrics.description: The senex iratus—an enraged, gullible father figure—is central to the alazon group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by rages, threats, obsessions, and gullibility; related to demonic romance figures (e.g., Polyphemus). Functions as an obstacle whose gullibility and rage drive comic complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miles gloriosus as alazon variant
rubrics_metrics.description: The miles gloriosus is a braggart who is chiefly a man of words, not deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued by dramatists for comic usefulness; his boastfulness and cowardice make him easier to exploit for plot and comedy than a tight-lipped hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedant, fop, coxcomb and 'humors' types
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedant, fop/coxcomb, and other 'humors' are recognized alazon/entertaining types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stock comic characters (e.g., pedant as occult-student in Renaissance comedy) provide predictable comic behavior and are standard tools for dramatists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity and forms of female alazon
rubrics_metrics.description: Female alazon is rare but exists in forms like the shrew or the precieuse ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Female alazon may appear as a female miles gloriosus or pedant; often the 'menace' or siren who obstructs the heroine appears more in melodrama/romance than in pure comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero as eiron: played down character
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic hero is often an eiron figure because the dramatist plays him down and makes him neutral or unformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatists intentionally under-characterize the hero to allow comic resolution to arise from situations and other players rather than heroic psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroine as eiron / muta persona
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroine is often played down and may function as a muta persona (stage prop) until a device (e.g., disguise) enables cognitio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a heroine disguises herself or engineers the recognition, she performs the cognitio that resolves the comic plot (the 'she stoops to conquer' variant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tricky slave / scheming valet / gracioso (vice) as eiron architect
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheming intermediary (tricky slave, valet, gracioso, vice) hatches the schemes that produce the hero's victory; often the 'architectus' of comic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Plautine tricky slave, Shakespeare's Puck/Ariel, Figaro, Leporello, Jeeves. The type can evolve into detective-like figures; may have buffoon affiliations. Often motivated by reward (e.g., freedom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice as spirit of comedy and use of disguise
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice often embodies the spirit of comedy and frequently uses disguise as a dramatic device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The vice can be spiritual (Puck, Ariel), acts from love of mischief, and engages in disguises (e.g., Brainworm's metamorphoses; 'Enter invisible' directions). Disguise often signals this type to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retreating paternal eiron (withdraw-and-return type)
rubrics_metrics.description: An older figure who begins action by withdrawing and ends it by returning; often a father testing his son.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type initiates a comic experiment by absence and later provides resolution on return (e.g., Duke in Measure for Measure, Lovewit in The Alchemist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice acting under orders / Prospero figure
rubrics_metrics.description: In some plays the vice acts under orders from an older authority (a Prospero-type) who engineers the comic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospero-like figures arrange schemes off-stage or by manipulation; sometimes the vice's apparent autonomy is actually directed by such a paternal figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffoon/entertainer types and festive function
rubrics_metrics.description: Buffoon types (professional fools, clowns, parasites, cooks, mad hosts) primarily increase festivity rather than propel plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roles include parasite (talks appetite), cook (master of ceremonies), loquacious hosts (Simon Eyre, mad host), and combinations with vice (Mosca). They connect comedy to the revel/chōros/komos tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parasite and cook conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The parasite entertains by appetite talk; the cook acts as on-stage master of ceremonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These figures derive from Greek Middle Comedy and often serve as centers for comic mood rather than plot resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agroikos / churl / rustic (refuser of festivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agroikos means churlish or rustic; functions as refuser of festivity, killjoy, or straight man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roles include misers, snobs, prigs (e.g., Malvolio), or rustic 'rubes' who either oppose festivity or represent pastoral virtues (Corin). Position relative to comic mood varies by context (urban vs pastoral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain dealer / outspoken moralist
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain dealer is an outspoken advocate of moral norm who may have audience sympathy and performs a chorus-like role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful in ironic comedies to clarify social norm; may become a malcontent or railer in darker tones (e.g., Cleante in Tartuffe; Thersites as negative variant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's emotional counterparts to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Where tragedy raises pity and fear, comedy raises sympathy and ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy uses social/moral judgment functionally: it elicits sympathy for the eiron and ridicule for the alazon, casting these emotions out as part of resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of comic structure across tones
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic structural patterns and characterization remain largely the same across a range from savage irony to dreamy romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite differences in tone or author's opinions, the archetypal forms (types, contests, recognitions) persist throughout variations in comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of ritual death (near-tragic crisis in comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comic narratives approach a potentially tragic crisis near the end — a 'point of ritual death' — before rapidly reversing into comic resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions like a stretto in music: may be literal (near death, legal ruin) or tonal (sudden seriousness). Examples: Tom Jones accused of crimes before revelation; Smollett's carriage accident leading to cognitio; comic clowns' mask-dropping speeches showing beaten faces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic comedy phase (Phase 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 1 (most ironic): a humorous society triumphs or remains undefeated; speculum consuetudinis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings may affirm the humorous society (e.g., The Alchemist) or present disintegration without replacement (e.g., Heartbreak House, Chekhov), producing different intensities of irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonic/tragic background in ironic comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ironic comedy is often close to demonic or brutal realities (threats of flogging, death), making the escape to comedy feel like deliverance from real peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plautus and others literalize harsh punishments onstage; modern analogues include symbolic instruments of doom. Comic reversal thus often narrowly averts serious catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quixotic comedy phase (Phase 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 2 (quixotic): hero or constructed society is an illusion that ultimately fails to impose itself on reality; hero escapes or runs away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phase examines hero-as-illusion (like Quixote); dramatic examples include The Wild Duck and subordinate quixotic themes in other plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal/maturational comedy phase (Phase 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 3 (normal): senex iratus yields to a young man's desires; cognitio resolves identity/marriage complications; comic norm is asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical elements include recognition scenes, sorting of brides/sisters/parents/foster-parents, Oedipal tensions (hero replacing father), and doubling of characters (pairs of young men/women or senex doubles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Green world / romantic comedy phase (Phase 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 4: the play moves into a 'green world' — a second, idealized social plane where metamorphosis and comic resolution occur, then returns to the normal world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Green world symbolizes victory of summer over winter; examples include the Forest of Arden, Windsor Forest, Belmont's mysterious house. Not present in more ironic/problem comedies (All's Well, Measure for Measure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroine-as-Proserpine / ritual assault and rebirth motif
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic comedy frequently uses a ritual assault on a central female figure (disguise, indignity) culminating in rebirth/recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heroine often disguises as a boy to achieve cognitio; this motif runs from Menander through Shakespeare to soap operas (the 'put the heroine behind the eight-ball' formula). It corresponds to fertility/Proserpine myths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic/Arcadian phase (Phase 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 5: more romantic and pensive — less purely festive, can contain tragedy; audience perspective is raised above the action into an ordered upper world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romances in this phase can include tragic elements and metamorphosis (e.g., The Winter's Tale). 'Sea' comedies (A Comedy of Errors, Twelfth Night, Pericles, The Tempest) are grouped here; action may take place entirely in the second world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collapse/disintegration phase (Phase 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase 6: collapse and disintegration of the comic society; comic units become small/esoteric and the mood becomes solitary, 'penseroso', or oracular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settings shift to secret places, islands, moonlit forests; tone moves toward ghost stories, thrillers, Gothic romance or dilettante withdrawal (e.g., A Rebours). Mythic return-to-the-womb motifs may appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-stage structure of romance (quest: agon, pathos, anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete romance (successful quest) has three main stages: the perilous journey/minor adventures; the crucial struggle or death-struggle; and the exaltation/recognition of the hero (agon, pathos, anagnorisis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite rhythm mirrors ritual death-and-rebirth motifs (e.g., three-day death/resurrection myth cycles) and often shows up in motifs like the 'third son' or success on a third attempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance as sequential, processional, adventure-based form
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance's essential element of plot is adventure, making it naturally sequential and processional; often a series of minor adventures leading to the climacteric quest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In popular/serial forms the hero can remain static (comic strips); literary romance imposes a climactic quest to provide form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero vs antagonist polarity and seasonal/mythic mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic narratives concentrate values in a hero (messianic/deliverer) and an antagonist (demonic); the hero maps to spring/youth/fertility, the enemy to winter/old age/sterility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As romances approach myth, the hero acquires divine attributes and the enemy demonic ones. The conflict is dialectical and centralizes reader sympathy around the hero.
